overview.text: Spiders are arachnids in the order Araneae. Unlike insects, they have eight legs, two main body regions, and no antennae. They are predators, but they do not all hunt alike: some wait in webs, while others ambush or chase prey. All spiders produce silk from spinnerets near the rear of the abdomen; webs are only one use, alongside egg coverings, shelters, and safety draglines. Orb webs, a familiar design, have radiating support threads and spiral capture threads, but spider webs take many forms. By capturing insects through varied hunting strategies, spiders play a useful role in ecosystems.

key_facts.text: Spiders belong to the arachnid order Araneae; arachnids also include mites, ticks, and scorpions.
A spider’s body has two main regions and eight legs; unlike insects, spiders have no antennae.
All spiders produce silk, but not all build webs to catch prey; jumping spiders can pursue prey, and crab spiders can ambush it.
Spinnerets on the abdomen produce silk, which can harden in air and serve uses such as egg cases, shelters, draglines, and webs.
Orb webs use radiating threads and spiral threads; other web designs include tangles, sheets, and spring traps.
